name: HOLLOW SIGNAL // RADIO
description:
HOLLOW SIGNAL // RADIO is not a label in any conventional sense — it has no registration, no physical address that persists longer than six weeks, and no staff who use their legal names on air. What it has is a transmitter array that has been rebuilt eleven times since 2211, a rotating cast of DJs and live performers who broadcast from rooftops, flooded basement levels, and the upper decks of decommissioned transit barges, and a listener base in the Shelf and lower Circuit that treats its signal like a lifeline. The station operates on a pirate frequency that drifts deliberately to avoid Vantablack's broadcast compliance scanners, announced each week through a coded image posted to encrypted mesh boards: a heron silhouette over varying numbers of horizontal lines indicating the new frequency band.

Hollow Signal's 'label' function emerged organically — artists who performed live on-air began leaving data chips with the rotating broadcast crew, who would play them between live sets, and listeners began requesting physical copies. Now the station maintains an informal catalog of several hundred releases, all distributed through a chip-trading network that operates through Shelf markets, Circuit worker pubs, and a handful of sympathetic Tier 3 record shops that keep the chips under the counter. The music is raw, political, and technically diverse — live improvisation sessions sit alongside carefully engineered protest tracks and field recordings from Shelf infrastructure spaces. No compliance certification has ever been sought or granted.
creator: Unknown founding collective (attributed to 'the Heron crew,' identity disputed and deliberately obscured)
genre: Shelf protest, Raw neural broadcast, Live improvisation, Field recording, Pirate circuit folk
audience: Shelf residents, lower Circuit workers, labor radicals, anti-corporate activists, pirate media enthusiasts across all tiers
cultural_impact: Hollow Signal has been declared illegal by GLMZ's broadcast authority on four separate occasions, each declaration accompanied by a sweep that destroyed the current transmitter and failed to locate the crew. The station's cultural weight in the Shelf is difficult to overstate — for communities with no reliable licensed media that speaks to their experience, Hollow Signal is not entertainment but infrastructure. Its broadcasts have announced labor actions, warned of corporate security sweeps, and served as the venue for publicly airing grievances that Vantablack's censorship apparatus would never permit on licensed channels. The station's signal has been detected as far up as Tier 3, where a small but devoted listenership tunes in specifically because it is forbidden.
known_fans: Lower Circuit residents who grew up with the signal
Certain sympathetic Tier 2 transit workers who leave receivers running on overnight shifts
story_hooks: Vantablack's compliance division has deployed a new frequency-tracking algorithm that has narrowed Hollow Signal's broadcast location to a three-block radius in the Shelf's Kazan waterfront. The crew has 48 hours before a sweep team arrives. Someone needs to get a warning through, but the station's own mesh contact list may have been compromised.

A Hollow Signal broadcast from three weeks ago contained seventeen seconds of audio that, when spectrographically analyzed, reveals embedded coordinates — not to a broadcast location, but to a flooded sub-basement in a Tier 2 corporate district. No one in the current crew claims to have put it there. Someone used the station's signal to hide a message, and whoever it was for hasn't retrieved it yet.

A Tier 4 investigative journalist wants to do an authorized profile on Hollow Signal — arguing the publicity would make the station harder to shut down by raising its profile. The crew is deeply divided. Half believe exposure is protection. Half believe it's exactly how the compliance division would want to flush them out.
